summary: Explains that TCP connections are vulnerable to forged reset (RST) packets, especially between well-known endpoints on predictable ports, such as BGP sessions. It discusses ways to make such attacks harder and the tradeoffs involved. It is informational guidance, not a new protocol.

eli5.summary: Someone can fake a note that says hang up the call. This explains ways to make it harder for fakers to cut off other people's connections.

questions: how to defend against tcp reset attacks

how to defend against tcp rst spoofing

subtitle: Why forged TCP reset packets became a real threat to long-lived connections like BGP, and the ways to defend.

tldr.problem: An attacker who is not on the path can forge a TCP reset (RST) with a spoofed source address and kill a connection, and larger receive windows make a valid guess far easier.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC works out how the exposure grows with the square of bandwidth, then compares transport-layer fixes (TCP/MD5, RST window attenuation, timestamps), network-layer fixes (address filtering, TTL checks, IPsec) and ICMP checks.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational survey with no new protocol. It concludes no solution is free of drawbacks and favors network-layer defenses against identity spoofing.

today: RFC 4953 is an Informational RFC from July 2007. The unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated, and it states that it describes no new standard.

sections.title: The Problem: Spoofed Resets
sections.content:
The RFC was prompted by a vulnerability in BGP connections between core routers. A third party who is off-path (cannot see the traffic) can send a reset (RST) segment with a forged source address and terminate the TCP connection. BGP routers may react by restarting the connection or by deciding the peer is unreachable and flushing its routes, which amplifies the damage.

The attack is not new: it was documented nearly six years earlier and was the reason TCP/MD5 was developed. The RFC adds the observation that susceptibility grows with the square of the bandwidth. It focuses on spoofed TCP segments and also discusses related ICMP spoofing.
sections.eli5: Someone far away pretends to be one of the two friends on the phone and says goodbye for them. The call drops, and the phone company may think a line is broken.

sections.title: Why Reset Attacks Got Easier
sections.content:
Most TCP connections are protected by obscurity: addresses, ports and sequence numbers are hard to know and connections are short-lived. BGP is an exception. Both endpoints can be well known, the destination port is fixed, and even when the source port is not fixed there are only about 65,000 to try. Connections are also long-lived.

The last barrier is the sequence number. TCP accepts a RST if its sequence number falls anywhere inside the receive window. When the window is small (under 35,000 bytes), the odds of a blind guess are 1 in 57,000. But on fast paths the receive window is tuned to match the bandwidth-delay product, so the window covers a large share of the 32-bit space.

Because the window grows with bandwidth and an attacker's sending rate also grows with bandwidth, the exposure is squared. The RFC's table shows that at 10 Gbps about 35 RSTs would suffice, taking 1 microsecond, while at 1 Mbps it takes 343,598 RSTs and about 2 minutes. Router buffers of 128 KB, 32 KB or 4 KB lower the exposure but do not remove it.
sections.eli5: If a lock has only a few possible codes, you can try them all quickly. Faster networks make the window of acceptable codes bigger, so a lucky guess comes much sooner.

sections.title: Transport-Layer Defenses
sections.content:
TCP MD5 uses a pre-shared key to sign the whole segment, including RSTs. It is widely deployed in routers but considered impractical for wide use because of the keys it needs, and it is costly to compute. The RFC also notes concerns about MD5 collision attacks.

RST window attenuation accepts a RST only if its sequence number matches the expected next one, so the attacker needs up to 2^32 guesses regardless of window size. A mismatched RST triggers a zero-length ACK so a genuine sender can retry. It is incrementally deployable but changes TCP control processing. Variants require the initial sequence number in the RST, widen the sequence space from 32 to 64 bits, or shrink the receive window, which can reduce throughput.

TCP timestamp authentication uses the timestamp option as a check, but its values can be easy to guess. All these are forms of cookies: clear-text ones stop off-path attackers only, while MD5 signatures act like one-time cookies. SCTP and DCCP already use cookies, but each protocol must be fixed separately as new attacks appear.
sections.eli5: You can make the password longer, ask for a secret handshake, or only allow one exact word. Each helps, but each one means changing how everyone talks.

sections.title: Network-Layer Defenses
sections.content:
Address filtering drops packets whose source address could not come from where they entered, typically at the border of an autonomous system. It only works if every border router does it, so it cannot protect a pair of hosts locally. A variant checks that the IP TTL is 255, which limits traffic to one hop away, but tunnels that do not decrement TTL can defeat it.

IPsec authenticates a packet's source and contents and protects all transport protocols. Its drawbacks are cost and key distribution: it relies on pre-shared keys, X.509 certificates or a trusted third party, which is hard for servers with anonymous clients or BGP routers with many peers. IKE can re-key automatically. The RFC points to work on keying without prior coordination so public servers can still benefit.

It also notes that application-layer security such as TLS or SSH cannot stop spoofed packets from resetting transport connections before the application checks data, and that link-layer security cannot authenticate the endpoint of a packet.
sections.eli5: A guard at the building entrance can check that visitors really come from where they claim. A secret badge system checks each visitor, but handing badges to everyone is a chore.

sections.title: ICMP and the Trade-offs
sections.content:
Spoofed ICMP messages can also reset a connection or attack path MTU, and some need even less validation than a spoofed TCP segment. Proposals include checking the sequence number of the TCP header carried inside the ICMP message, validating the TCP checksum first, and checking the TCP MD5 signature if present. Requiring ICMP to be in window may not be enough, and some networks filter all ICMP.

In its issues discussion the RFC compares layers. Transport solutions are per protocol and per connection, and authenticate late in packet processing. Network solutions give one shared mechanism early in processing. It suggests that for spoofing it may be enough to prove a sender is a party you have exchanged packets with, rather than proving who it is, and points to the Better Than Nothing Security (BTNS) work.
sections.eli5: Fake stop signs from a different kind of messenger can also stop the traffic. The same careful checking helps, but no single trick protects against everything.

sections.title: Security Considerations and Conclusions
sections.content:
The whole document is about resisting spoofing. Techniques relying on clear-text cookies, such as window sequence attenuation, do not protect against on-path attackers because valid values can be learned from earlier traffic. True authentication algorithms protect even on-path, since a hash behaves like a one-time cookie.

Spoofing is identity masquerading, so the authors believe the most appropriate solutions defeat it at the network layer, though addressing all layers is reasonable. NATs and other middleboxes that modify headers look like spoofing and complicate defenses; the RFC leaves this out of scope but notes that many critical connections such as BGP do not cross them.
sections.eli5: Simple secret words can be overheard by someone standing close. Strong checks cannot be copied, so they protect even from nearby snoops.
